narrative:
The model estimates you have a 34% chance of failing your final year. This is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your chances of passing.

The prediction is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. First, although you have had no past class failures (matching the average of students who passed), the model sees this as unexpectedly low given your other patterns and therefore does not give you as much credit for it as it usually would for students who ultimately succeed. Second, you do want to pursue higher education, which normally pushes predictions strongly toward passing; however, this positive signal is outweighed by the rest of your profile. Third, your father’s education level is secondary, which the model treats as a moderate negative factor compared with the higher education levels more commonly seen among parents of students who pass.

Taken together, these elements tipped the balance toward a fail prediction even though many parts of your background, such as strong family relationships, internet access, and wanting to continue studying, look favourable.

To improve, focus on the areas you can control now: increase your weekly study time beyond the two hours you currently spend (most students who pass study 2–5 hours), reduce absences (yours are already more than double the average of those who succeed), and consider extra academic support. Small, consistent changes in these habits can meaningfully raise your probability of passing.
